# Reader report — Cognition, "Factoring RSA-260" (cognition.com/blog/factoring-rsa-260)

**Read 2026-09-10, Session 21, from the Firecrawl scrape `page.md` in this folder (929 lines, 11,136 words).** Every claim below about the post is quoted from it, with the post's own section heading. Nothing here is from memory. The scraped text carries no byline; the author writes in the first person and thanks "my employer Cognition" and "Alex Lombardi for mathematical consultation and much editing" (Acknowledgments). Numbers and dates are reproduced as printed.

The sponsor's question was not "what did they factor" but "any insight in problem-solving that might be applicable to our RH program". This file records what the post says; the transfers are in `process-lessons.md` beside it.

## 1. The problem and the result

- **What was factored.** "RSA-260 (a 260 digit number) sets a new record for the largest publicly solved RSA Factoring Challenge problem" (opening). The number is printed in full with its two factors, each a 130-digit prime ("p130 × p130", Appendix 3 §8).
- **Prior record and context.** "The previous record, RSA-250, was set in February 2020. For reference, state-of-the-art RSA public keys contain 2048 bit (~617 digit) factoring problems, while 1024-bit (~309 digit) RSA was deprecated in 2013" (opening).
- **Elapsed time.** "About three weeks elapsed from first prompt to RSA-260 factors found" (Assorted reflections). The first prompt was sent "At August 13th 0:11:58 Pacific time" (Using Devin to optimize GNFS); "Factors were produced at 2026-09-03 01:48:57 UTC" (Appendix 2, Characters and square root). The RSA-260 run itself (polynomial selection to factors) is tabulated as 2026-08-18 12:14:19 to 2026-09-03 01:48:57 UTC, "1,344,878 s" of wall time (Running up the scaling ladder, table).
- **What was and was not new.** "The implementation was a significantly modified CADO-NFS. I report essentially no algorithmic advancements — implementing lattice sieving and sparse linear system solving on GPUs required only 'good old performance engineering' to take advantage of the preposterous memory systems of the GPU" (How did this happen?). The headline engineering claim: "my Devins built the world's highest-performance GPU lattice siever, which enables factoring numbers at 10x lower cost than the previous public state of the art" (opening).
- **The post's two stated takeaways** (opening, verbatim headings of the two bullets):
  1. "Hyperscalers or frontier AI labs could likely factor RSA-1024 numbers at a cost on the order of $30 million per number — and, with a bit more optimization, likely substantially less. On the other hand, RSA-2048 remains roughly a billion times harder than RSA-1024 and does not appear to be meaningfully affected by this work."
  2. "Devin is a sufficiently powerful software engineer to solve a challenging problem at the intersection of computational number theory and GPU performance engineering. My role was primarily to set priorities, establish benchmarks, and recognize when work was going off-track. Devin otherwise autonomously handled measurements, cluster operations, and optimization end-to-end. This substituted for what would likely have been a multi-month effort by a team of highly specialized domain experts."
- **The post's conclusion sentence.** "In conclusion, the barrier to entry for cryptanalytic work, other computational mathematics more broadly, and likely most large-scale scientific computing research, is far lower than it used to be" (opening).
- **Security reading, in the post's words.** "Of course, **the fact that RSA-1024 is insecure is not news.**" The three developments the post claims are "(1) a potentially lower cost (in dollars and time) for the factorization, (2) potentially more parties capable of performing the factorizations (you just need enough GPUs rather than making specialized hardware), and (3) **the relative ease with which non-cryptographers can now work on speeding up factoring**" (Cost estimates). And: "I emphasize that the efficiency gains have little impact on the feasibility of factoring RSA-2048-sized numbers with GNFS" (Cost estimates).

## 2. Cost and compute figures, as printed

- **Total.** "In total, I estimate that this factorization cost about 4,900 GPU-days, or 13.5 GPU-years, which is about $400k at current market prices" (Cost estimates). Appendix 1 tabulates RSA-260 at "13.5" GPU-years, "414k*" dollars, with the footnote "Costs assume $0.08/CPU core-hour, $3.50/GPU-hour."
- **Breakdown** (Cost estimates):
  - "643 GPU-days in polynomial selection (this is anomalously high basically due to operator incompetence)"
  - "3,813 GPU-days sieving"
  - "467 GPU-days linear system solving (of which about 7% failed to make progress due to crashes or preemption by more important work)"
- **Where the compute came from.** "The factorization ran at no marginal cost on spare or fragmented compute that couldn't be used for other purposes" (Factoring on spare compute). "I did this as a side project using a single-digit percentage of our cluster, in the course of optimizing our job scheduler to improve allocations to use disaggregated compute" (Cost estimates). The spare compute exists because "some racks may end up with an idle node or two; sometimes jobs request spare nodes to accommodate failover, or jobs might need even numbers of computers on a rack that has only 17. For us, these inefficiencies amount to a single-digit percentage of overall compute" (Factoring on spare compute).
- **Why sieving fit that compute.** "Lattice sieving is embarrassingly parallel over billions of small work units, can make progress using single nodes at a time, and is safe to preempt instantly. It is also the most computationally expensive part of GNFS" (Factoring on spare compute). "all prior public GNFS factorization records used only CPUs for lattice sieving; indeed, due to challenges of efficiently implementing lattice sieving on GPUs, for a long time it was not clear that GPU lattice sieving could be more cost-effective overall" (same section).
- **Extrapolation.** "RSA-1024 is equivalent to 309 digits; according to standard GNFS scaling this is merely 78x more computation than RSA-260. I estimate the cost of factoring RSA-1024 at market GPU prices to be roughly $30M" (Cost estimates). "I know for a fact that the current implementation remains significantly suboptimal; I would not be surprised if moderate further work could reduce the cost of factoring RSA-1024 by another multiple of 2" (same). Appendix 1 gives RSA-2048 as "91.2B×" RSA-260, "1.23 × 10¹²*" GPU-years, "3.77 × 10¹⁶*" dollars (asterisk = estimated).
- **Agent-side cost.** "In retrospect, Devin claims that I sent 82,702 words (502,887 characters) in 3,328 messages across 192 sessions out of 233 used for factoring (totaling 14,450 ACUs). Of these, Devins themselves started 101 child sessions, and 36 received no intervention from me at all" (What did Devin still need me (or other humans) for?). The post does not convert ACUs to dollars.

## 3. The computation pipeline, as the post describes it

The post's own framing: "modern GNFS implementations consist of a few stages run sequentially: polynomial selection, lattice sieving, and linear system solving" (Cost estimates), followed by characters and square root (Appendix 2).

### 3a. Polynomial selection
- Role: "Polynomial selection fixes the number field over which the algorithm is run. The choice of polynomial controls a constant-factor speedup on the lattice sieving step. It's therefore typically worth spending a fixed fraction (~5%) of overall sieving compute finding a 'good' polynomial" (GNFS optimizations (high-level)). "There was little technical innovation here; we adapted CADO's stage-1 polynomial selection to GPUs (resulting in `gps1`), using also some kernel equipment from msieve's well-optimized stage-1 polynomial selection."
- What actually happened on RSA-260: "Polynomial selection began on 2026-08-18 at 12:14:19 UTC. The search was irregular and a bit ad-hoc; it covered several runs over different admin/admax ranges, prime bounds P, and incr values. Search parameters shifted as benchmark results were produced, and I wasted much search time on unproductive ranges due to incorrect benchmark interpretation. A significant suboptimality of this run was spending too much time in polynomial selection; we could have searched the intended range in 1 day rather than 2.5, and it probably would have been worth it to spend only 12 hours searching less than the intended range" (Appendix 2, Polynomial selection).
- Scale: "The four stage-1 runs that produced every trial-sieved polynomial used 15,424 GPU-hours or 643 GPU-days", producing "83,557,723" polynomials of which "18,333" were root-optimized (Appendix 2 table). "We trial sieved a total of 22 distinct polynomials": "the top 5 by MurphyE among those we had available as of 2026-08-19 10:53 … then a further 17 selected as a union of the top 10 by each of four scores MurphyE, CADO's E, E'sigma, and E'chi2 … as of 2026-08-21 06:08:18".
- Outcome: the chosen polynomial is "degree 6, skew 3,226,459, MurphyE 6.633e-10". "The second-best trial-sieved polynomial (c260-r2) had MurphyE 6.215e-10 and gave 1-2% lower yield. The best of the first five by MurphyE (c260-p1) had 5.674e-10 and gave 13-16% lower yield" (Appendix 2).

### 3b. Lattice sieving on GPU
- Role and the technical crux: "The bulk of the GNFS computational effort is in lattice sieving. The goal of lattice sieving is to produce lots (8.3 billion in our case) of sparse linear relations over GF(2) … Lattice sieving is also embarrassingly parallel over work items called 'special q's, but each work item requires performing a large number of read/writes at (for our purposes) pseudorandom locations in a large array; **handling this was the primary technical challenge in optimizing sieving**" (GNFS optimizations (high-level)).
- The run: "Sieving began on 2026-08-22 at 10:01:12 UTC and reached target at 2026-08-30 07:26:15 UTC … Sieving wallclock time was 189.5 hours = 7.9 days." Parameters "lpb0/lpb1 = 36/37 … lim0 = lim1 = 2^31, mfb0/mfb1 = 72/111, ncurves 50/35, A = 33, sqside = 1"; "a total of 632,249 workunits. We used a special q range of 60,000 per workunit so they would take about 10 minutes" (Appendix 2, Sieving).
- Character of the run: "Sieving was relatively drama-free. We upgraded the siever twice during this process, gaining 14-17% performance vs. the start of sieving. Measuring end-to-end workunit times as the median interval between consecutive uploads from one GPU, our GB200s went from 585 s to 486s, GB300s from 586s to 504s, and B200s from 628s to 541s. Overall sieving time was 3,813 GPU-days."
- Output: "we obtained 13,849,985,589 raw relations for filtering (shy of the 13.85B target because four files were truncated after running out of disk space), which filtered down to 8,298,749,059 unique relations (40.1% duplicates), and 3,991,449 free relations."

### 3c. Filtering and linear algebra
- Filtering: "Dedup/purge/merge/filter took 4 hours end-to-end (after a run crashed 2 hours in) on 176 threads of a 192-vCPU node and produced a 656,182,601 x 656,182,189 matrix with 98,431,741,898 nonzeros at density 150 per row" (Appendix 2, Linear algebra).
- Method: "we pack these relations into a large matrix over GF(2) and use linear system solving to find a linear dependence. At this scale, linear system solving is typically distributed and requires a lot of communication bandwidth; this is available in spades over Infiniband and NVLink. The block Wiedemann algorithm permits relaxing the communication constraint somewhat, and the particular implementation in CADO-NFS is also susceptible to optimization and running on GPUs, which we undertook" (GNFS optimizations (high-level)).
- How the optimization went: "We optimized the linear algebra while sieving proceeded. Optimization was turbulent because we simultaneously co-optimized matrix params, solver layout, and code targeting speculative final matrix properties. For representative test inputs, we eventually converged on a few matrices formed using optimized `fake_rels`. This fed back into sieving: changes to linear algebra performance (and departure from trial sieving yield estimates) nudged the relation target a couple of times. It is unclear to me how far we were from optimal overall, but I halted optimization when a 48-hour linear algebra run seemed within reach" (Appendix 2, Linear algebra).
- The run: "Linear algebra began on 2026-08-30 15:45:10 UTC. Dispatch/prep/secure took 4.4 hours. `krylov` ran 2,564,096 iterations on each of two width-256 sequences (m = n = 512), taking 0.045 to 0.102 s per iteration depending on available compute. We saved checkpoints every 8,192 iterations and kept every fourth one to enable parallelizing `mksol` … `krylov` was done at 2026-09-02 02:38:14 UTC. `lingen` took 3.5 hours on a single GB200 node with 4 GPUs; multiple attempts were pre-empted so this phase took 7 hours overall. We ran 40 `mksol` ranges across two clusters … Gather took 9m04s on a 2x2 grid and wrote 64 kernel vectors."
- Correctness checks run alongside: "To confirm the correctness of the optimized implementation, which had not been tested on any smaller scale before starting the run, we factored (11^331 - 1)/10 (C344) end-to-end while `krylov` ran. As another check, in parallel with `krylov`, we also ran CADO's `bwccheck` over every V checkpoint pair. CADO's normal in-`krylov` check went off about 14 hours into the run; we re-ran that interval and continued the run correctly."
- Infrastructure friction: "Unlike sieving, linear algebra requires all of its workers to remain up. Consequently it was fatally preempted frequently and we had to develop a somewhat complex placement script to constantly fit the best shape possible to the available compute." The planned "dedicated cliques" were not available "due to the requirements of higher-priority workloads".

### 3d. Characters and square root
- "Normally this step requires relatively inconsiderable computational effort, but in the RSA-260 run took 12 hours end-to-end after running into some trouble. Due to the size of the rational product (1.76e11 bits), `sqrt` overflowed the `mpz_t` limb counter and aborted. Devin rebuilt `sqrt` three times (first using GMP's `mpn` functions and then also parallel Karatsuba on CPU); the version that ultimately produced the factors used GPU-accelerated NTT multiplication and finished in 88 minutes" (Appendix 2, Characters and square root).

### 3e. What was modified in CADO-NFS
- "Overall, Devin substantially modified almost every piece, including modifying a couple of interfaces": a GPU stage-1 polyselect "with components from msieve"; "A GPU-optimized lattice siever based on `las`"; "An optimized CADO head to handle the workunit volume"; "Parallelized and optimized dup/purge and fused merge/replay programs"; "A new GPU-optimized block Wiedemann implementation"; "GPU-accelerated sqrt"; "Associated run scripts" (GNFS optimizations (high-level)). "The only untouched programs in the CADO-NFS pipeline were: `cado-nfs.py` itself, `polyselect_ropt` (stage-2 polynomial selection), `makefb`, and `dup1`. We even had to optimize `fake_rels` to get reasonable performance for synthetic inputs of the needed sizes."

## 4. The human–agent workflow, as the post describes it

### 4a. The opening prompt and the first night
- "At August 13th 0:11:58 Pacific time I aimed Devin at producing a drop-in replacement for `las`, the CPU lattice siever of CADO-NFS" (Using Devin to optimize GNFS). The prompt is printed in full; its operative sentences: "I'd like you to develop a fast GPU lattice siever. This has historically been difficult with present techniques because optimizations for CPU lattice sieving employ a lot of conditional branching and complex memory access patterns, and the intersection of GPU kernel-writing experts and number field theory experts is quite small. However, the higher total memory bandwidth available in a GPU promises a higher performance ceiling. And that intersection now contains you." It grants one GPU box for measurement ("use GPU only for performance testing and shut it down between measurements"), fixes the acceptance criterion ("a drop-in replacement for the siever step of CADO-NFS"), and sets the loop ("Iterate until you exceed the performance of the CPU lattice siever").
- "Two hours later I added that `glas` (GPU `las`, of course) should be able to handle the parameters used for RSA-250. Then I went to bed. I woke up to find that, after another 7 hours of iteration, Devin had succeeded" (same section).
- "Over the subsequent week I drove Devin to optimize lattice sieving, then the rest of the GNFS pipeline."

### 4b. Parallel sessions, duration, cadence
- "I drove several parallel Devins. Across the 3-week duration of the project, I had an average of 3 and a maximum of 18 concurrent Devin sessions running" (The optimization workflow).
- Two kinds of session: "iteratively optimizing an individual component — designing and running experiments, interpreting results, selecting target improvements, implementing them, and repeating" and "managing end-to-end factorization runs on the cluster — exercising the whole pipeline and supporting scripts, revealing the most important inefficiencies (errors, utilization, performance) for further optimization" (same).
- Human cadence: "I interacted with this optimization loop once every couple of hours, alternating with talking to other Devin sessions for my regular work" (same).
- Platform properties the post credits: "sessions are persistent and independent from my computer, parallelization is straightforward, sandboxing prevents interference between independent workstreams, and sessions can run autonomously for weeks" (same).
- Session accounting (repeated from §2): "3,328 messages across 192 sessions out of 233 used for factoring (totaling 14,450 ACUs). Of these, Devins themselves started 101 child sessions, and 36 received no intervention from me at all" (What did Devin still need me (or other humans) for?).

### 4c. What the agents did
- "Devin handled substantial portions of: choosing and tuning parameters for sieving and linear system solving (though using benchmarking equipment that I had to help bootstrap); generating/optimizing polynomial selections (again, with varying degrees of difficulty); running the iterative optimization loop; debugging (naturally); setting up and optimizing the processing scripts; orchestrating large-scale computation on the cluster" (The optimization workflow, bullets joined).
- "We already knew that Devin was effective at GPU programming, experimentation, and cluster management for ML-relevant workloads, but lattice sieving and GNFS are fairly different; I found Devin's ability to generalize here quite impressive" (same).

### 4d. What the human did — the post's own list
The post's answer to "What did Devin still need me (or other humans) for?" is "Somehow, the answer seems to be: still a lot." It names "executive function, talking through and sanity-checking what it was doing, to wit:" and lists six items, verbatim:
1. "setting a hierarchy of goals and keeping Devin properly scoped"
2. "recognizing when Devin was doing something unproductive and redirecting ('you don't need to take that measurement')"
3. "recognizing repeated inefficiencies in Devin's workflows ('you can amortize this setup work')"
4. "pointing out untried directions ('make sure the GPU never blocks on the CPU', 'can you use NVLink SHARP here?')"
5. "organizing experimental frameworks and results ('do measurements this way and find previous results here, don't cook up new incomparable approaches every time')"
6. "catching when Devin prematurely gave up on a direction"

And the post's self-assessment of which mattered most: "While in retrospect I appear to have supplied a couple of specific technical insights, my biggest contribution was probably to handhold the creation of a unified set of measured results, benchmarks, and performance estimators, which evidently were not otherwise going to self-assemble. This enabled Devin to more easily run and understand measurements, and me to understand the extent of progress and where more improvements were needed."

### 4e. What the human did not know
- "N.B. I understand these components only in the same way a mid-level car hobbyist might understand car components: their approximate role in the overall system, their effects on performance, some tradeoffs of making changes, and what good operation and usage looks like — but not the underlying physics, nor how to fabricate the component from raw materials. That's to say that I do not understand much of the underlying mathematics. I can tell you that polynomial selection provides a constant factor on lattice sieving yield; I cannot tell you how the polynomial is used in the siever. In this field I am far from an expert!" (GNFS optimizations (high-level)).
- The author does describe a decade of factoring as a hobby: "because I've enjoyed factoring numbers as a hobby for the past ten years or so" (opening), and dedicates the post "to the whole online factoring community — GIMPS, mersenneforum, FactorDB, GPU to 72, and the rest" (Acknowledgments).

### 4f. The scaffold: CADO-NFS and the human-engineered decomposition
- "**this effort would not have been possible without CADO-NFS.** CADO-NFS is an advanced, robust, open source implementation of GNFS that was used in many previous records and also by the factoring hobbyist community. It provided all the relevant techniques, the pipeline stages and their interfaces, and a reference CPU implementation. Using those, I could have the Devin swarm optimize programs roughly independently and compare the outputs with the originals. Like in many other cases, I believe that the human-engineered decomposition of the problem was essential to enabling the agents to make progress" (What did Devin still need me (or other humans) for?).
- "In fact, I noticed that the further the codebase got from upstream CADO-NFS, the more confused the agents became. This could be attributed to accumulating complexity, but I wonder whether CADO-NFS's presence in pre-training is also relevant here" (same).

### 4g. The scaling ladder
- "This workflow permitted an incredible rate of progress that I (and even Devin itself) could barely keep up with. For the first five days we ran up a scaling ladder. By the end of this, factoring a 190-digit number took the same amount of time as a 157-digit number had at the start — a little over 3 hours" (Running up the scaling ladder).
- The ladder, as tabulated (Target — wall time): C155 "7,988 s (including a 1,412 s gap from head crash testing)"; C157 "11,486 s"; C173 "40,666 s"; C175 "30,239 s"; C190 (near-repdigit) "19,060 s"; C201 "57,075 s"; C311 = (179^139 − 1)/178 "51,542 s"; C190 (random semiprime, "just to startle a Devin who randomly generated a semiprime") "11,443 s"; C344 = (11^331 − 1)/10 "132,950 s"; RSA-260 "1,344,878 s". Dates run 2026-08-14 through 2026-09-03. Appendix 3 adds two post-RSA-260 runs: C337 (cofactor of 2^1207 − 1, "658" GPU-days) and "C385, 2^1277 - 1 — a new record for SNFS" ("2,423" GPU-days, finished 2026-09-08 11:08:57 UTC).
- The skipped rung, in the post's words: "After factoring the C311 (which was roughly equivalent in difficulty to GNFS on a 216-digit number), it would have been safer to proceed by factoring a 230-digit equivalent difficulty number in order to cross the remaining couple of orders of magnitude. But I estimated that RSA-260 could be done in under a month and therefore had already begun polynomial selection, even though I knew the linear algebra remained significantly underoptimized" (Running up the scaling ladder).
- Appendix 3 also records, for C337 and C385, the alternative polynomials rejected by trial sieving with measured percentages ("relations per 5,000-q window relative to the sextic at lpb 37/37, q = 2e9 / 8e9 / 32e9 / 128e9: octic x^8 - 2 … -55% / -57% / -66% / -71%; septic … -4% / -17% / -22% / -32%; quintic … -62% / -54% / -48% / -39%"), and for C344 alternatives "rejected on norm estimates, not by trial sieving".

## 5. The post's own reflections and stated takeaways

- **Credit.** "What has happened here is strange to me. My name is on the result, but it's not clear to me how to apportion credit among myself, Devin, the hardware, and the world at large" (Assorted reflections). "For programming tasks, I think of current models and agents somewhat like a sewing machine or a loom. I push it along in some way; it evidently could not happen without me, but neither am I throwing the shuttle by hand."
- **Pace and the overhang.** "About three weeks elapsed from first prompt to RSA-260 factors found. The rate evinces a capability overhang whose extent we are only beginning to explore. I think we should not shy away from this exploration. In particular, if a problem can be solved via 'just programming', it seems worthwhile to attempt this immediately" (Assorted reflections).
- **Human understanding.** "In the past few days, we've also seen some impressive claimed results in mathematics, including a claimed solution to one of the Millennium Prize Problems. I share some concerns about a loss of human understanding. I did not learn as much about NFS or GPU programming as I could have expected to had I done this on my own, though likely more than I would have if I were not using Devin at all. It seems important to figure out how to globally allocate resources to maintain human understanding even when technology enables or incentivizes us to forgo this. At the same time, these tools may allow us to choose where deeper understanding is most valuable, explore further than any individual could previously reach, and expand the set of people who can make meaningful contributions. I see this work as an example in both directions" (Assorted reflections).
- **The closing exhortation of the summary.** "Exciting work beckons anywhere programming can be used to solve a research problem; I encourage all to be ambitious and explore what autonomous software engineering agents can do when applied to these fields!" (opening).
- **Denials.** "Contrary to some circulating claims, I did not factor RSA-260 by guessing and checking 130-digit prime numbers by hand. Cognition also has not yet built a multi-thousand-qubit quantum computer" (How did this happen?).

## 6. What the post does not say (recorded so no one infers it)

- It does not name the author in the scraped text, does not give a dollar figure for the Devin usage (ACUs only), and does not say what fraction of the 233 sessions produced code that shipped.
- It does not describe how the parallel sessions were kept from duplicating each other's work beyond "sandboxing prevents interference between independent workstreams" and the human's organizing of "experimental frameworks and results".
- It does not claim any new mathematics: "I report essentially no algorithmic advancements" (How did this happen?). It does not claim the human contributed mathematical insight; the "couple of specific technical insights" it cites are systems nudges ("make sure the GPU never blocks on the CPU", "can you use NVLink SHARP here?").
- It gives no verification statement for the factorization beyond the printed factors and FactorDB links (Appendix 3); the product can be checked by multiplication, which the post leaves implicit.
- The interactive charts in Appendix 2 did not survive the scrape as data; only their titles and axis text are present in `page.md` (lines 265–335).

## 7. Reading verdict for the program

The post is a faithful, numerically detailed account of a **computation** — a known algorithm (GNFS), a known reference implementation (CADO-NFS), a checkable answer (multiply the factors) — carried out by agents with a human supplying "executive function". Its problem-solving content is in §4d–4g above: a fixed benchmarking framework, a scaling ladder with a regretted skipped rung, a hierarchy of goals, redirection away from unproductive measurement, amortized setup, untried-direction nudges, catching premature give-up, correctness checks run alongside the main computation, and an honest waste ledger. The transfers, and where the computation/proof-search disanalogy bites, are in `process-lessons.md`.
